title: Merge Sorted Array
description: Brute force to optimized: copy and sort versus a three pointer merge from the back.

blocks.text: Given two sorted integer arrays nums1 and nums2, where nums1 has a length of m plus n and its last n slots are unused placeholders, merge nums2 into nums1 so that nums1 becomes one single sorted array of length m plus n.

blocks.caption: Merge from the back so the placeholder slots are filled before any real nums1 value could be overwritten

blocks.text: Given two sorted integer arrays nums1 and nums2, where nums1 has a length of m plus n and its last n slots are unused placeholders, merge nums2 into nums1 so that nums1 becomes one single sorted array of length m plus n.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Two Sorted Stacks of Papers Into One Tray
blocks.text: Like merging two already sorted stacks of numbered papers into a single tray with just enough room for both, working from the back of the tray forward so nothing already sorted in place ever gets overwritten by mistake.

blocks.caption: Merge two sorted arrays into one, using the extra space already reserved at the end

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Merging [1, 2, 3] with [2, 5, 6]","in sorted order","Both sub-arrays are already individually sorted, so merging them preserves overall sorted order by always taking the smaller available front element"],["Answer","[1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6]","Every element from both arrays appears exactly once, in fully sorted order"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["nums2 is empty, nothing to merge in","nums1 stays as is","With no elements to bring in from nums2, nums1's existing single real element is already the complete answer"],["Answer","[1]","nums1 requires no modification at all"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: nums1 = [0], m = 0, nums2 = [1], n = 1
When nums1 starts with no real elements of its own, the entire result is simply nums2 copied in, giving [1].

Before reaching for a full sort, notice both nums1's real elements and nums2 are already individually sorted, and merging two sorted sequences is a solved sub-problem: the classic merge step from merge sort, just with an unusual detail about where the destination space actually lives.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since both nums1's first m elements and nums2 are already sorted, a full re-sort of the combined array throws away that structure and redoes comparisons that a simple merge would never need to make.

Observation 2: The standard two-pointer merge, comparing the fronts of both sequences and taking the smaller each time, works whenever the destination has separate space from both sources; but here, nums1 is both a source and the destination, with its own real elements sitting in the exact slots that could be overwritten.

Observation 3: If merging proceeds from the front, placing a value at the current front slot could overwrite a nums1 element further along that has not been compared yet, corrupting the merge; but if merging proceeds from the back instead, every slot being written to has already had its original content compared and is safe to overwrite, since nothing later ever needs to read from a slot already filled in.

Observation 4: Merging from the back means comparing nums1's largest remaining candidate against nums2's largest remaining candidate, placing whichever is bigger into the current last open slot, and moving that side's pointer backward, mirroring the standard merge exactly, just running in reverse.

Whenever a merge must happen in place and the extra destination space sits at one end of the array being written into, merge from that end backward, so every slot is only ever written to after its original value has already been safely used or is no longer needed.

This exact "merge from the back to avoid overwrite" trick reappears whenever an in-place algorithm needs to write into the same array it is still reading from, and the safe direction to work in is determined by where the unused space actually is.
Copy every element of nums2 into the empty slots at the end of nums1, then sort the entire combined array from scratch.

items: Copy every element of nums2 into the placeholder slots at the end of nums1.
Sort the entire nums1 array.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The copy loop writes nums2's elements starting at index m, exactly the first placeholder slot, since indices 0 through m minus 1 already hold nums1's real elements that must not be touched yet.
Sorting is applied to the entire nums1 array only after all of nums2's elements have been copied in, since sorting a partially-filled array would produce a meaningless order.

No comparison logic is written explicitly at all here, since the built-in sort call handles establishing the correct order directly, at the cost of not exploiting either sub-array's existing sortedness.

blocks.text: Copying nums2 in and sorting the whole thing correctly produces a merged sorted array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((m plus n) log(m plus n)), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(log(m plus n)) to O(m plus n) depending on the sort implementation.
Limitation: both nums1 and nums2 are already individually sorted, and a full sort completely ignores that structure, doing far more comparisons than necessary.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force pays for a full sort's comparisons even though almost all of that ordering information already exists: both nums1's real prefix and nums2 arrive pre-sorted, so the only genuinely new work is interleaving two already-ordered sequences together, exactly what a linear merge does in O(m plus n) instead of O((m plus n) log(m plus n)). The one wrinkle is that nums1 doubles as the destination, with real data sitting in the same slots a naive forward merge would want to write into first. Flipping the merge to run backward sidesteps that entirely: the back slots are the placeholder ones nobody needs anymore, so filling them first, then working toward the front, never destroys a value before it has been read and compared.

Merge from the back instead of the front. Keep three pointers: one at the last real element of nums1, one at the last element of nums2, and one at the very last slot of the combined array. Repeatedly compare the two candidates and place the larger one at the current back slot, moving that pointer and the back slot pointer backward. Working from the back guarantees that placing a value never overwrites a nums1 element that has not been compared yet, which a forward merge could not guarantee without extra space.
Three pointers working from the back: nums1's last real element, nums2's last element, and the last slot of the combined array.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Compare","Result","Placed at the back","Why"],"rows":[["nums1[2]=3 vs nums2[2]=6","6 is larger","6 placed at index 5","6 is the largest remaining candidate from either side, so it correctly belongs in the very last position of the merged array"],["nums1[2]=3 vs nums2[1]=5","5 is larger","5 placed at index 4","With 6 already placed, 5 is now the largest remaining candidate, correctly taking the next-to-last position"],["nums1[2]=3 vs nums2[0]=2","3 is larger","3 placed at index 3","3 now beats nums2's remaining largest value, 2, so it takes this position instead"],["nums1[1]=2 vs nums2[0]=2","tie, either can go, place nums1's 2","2 placed at index 2","When values are equal, either one may be placed first without affecting the final sorted order, since both values are indistinguishable in the result"],["nums2 is now exhausted","remaining nums1 elements are already in place","done","Any values still left in nums1 at the front are, by construction, already smaller than everything placed so far and already sit in correct sorted order, needing no further action"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: merge from the back, placing the larger candidate into the last open slot

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m plus n), a single merge pass.
Space: O(1) extra, everything happens directly within nums1's existing space.

At every step, the value placed into the current back slot is guaranteed to be the largest value not yet placed anywhere, since it is chosen as the larger of the two current largest-remaining candidates from each side; placing values from largest to smallest, back to front, is exactly equivalent to placing them from smallest to largest, front to back, just approached in the opposite direction, and either produces the same correctly sorted result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pointer state","Meaning"],"rows":[["nums1 still has candidates and its current one is larger","nums1's current candidate is the larger one; place it and move that pointer backward"],["nums1 is exhausted, or its current candidate is not larger","nums2's current candidate is the larger one, or nums1 is exhausted; place it and move that pointer backward"]]}

items: i, j, and k start at m minus 1, n minus 1, and m plus n minus 1 respectively, exactly the last real index of nums1, the last index of nums2, and the last slot of the full combined array.
The loop condition checks only j, not i, since once nums2 is fully placed, anything remaining in nums1's front is already correctly sorted and needs no further copying.
nums1[i] is only compared once i's validity has already been confirmed, since comparing against an already-exhausted nums1 pointer would read invalid or stale data.
k decrements exactly once per loop iteration, regardless of which side's value was placed, since exactly one new value is always written to the merged array on every iteration.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (copy then full sort)","O((m+n) log(m+n))","O(log(m+n)) to O(m+n)","Ignores that both source sequences are already sorted, redoing comparisons a merge would never need"],["Optimized (merge from the back)","O(m+n)","O(1) extra","A single linear pass, reusing nums1's own trailing space as the destination"]]}

blocks.text: Merging from the back is the key trick whenever the destination array's extra space sits at the end rather than the beginning, since it avoids the overwrite problem a forward merge would otherwise create without an auxiliary array.

items: Merging from the front instead of the back, which would overwrite nums1 elements that have not been compared yet, corrupting the result before it can even be read.

Forgetting to continue copying remaining nums2 elements after nums1 is exhausted, though the reverse case, remaining nums1 elements after nums2 is exhausted, needs no action since those elements are already correctly in place at the front.
Comparing nums1's current candidate before confirming its pointer is still valid, which risks reading a stale or out-of-bounds value once nums1's real elements have all been placed.

items: Explain explicitly why merging backward avoids needing any extra space, since that insight is the entire point of this variant compared to a standard two array merge.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Merge in place where the destination array has trailing unused space" points toward merging from the back, filling the unused slots first so nothing already-real ever gets overwritten before being read.

items: How would this change if the unused space were at the front of nums1 instead of the back? The merge would need to proceed from the front forward instead, symmetric to this backward approach, always writing to the earliest unused slot.

What if nums1 and nums2 were both linked lists instead of arrays? The same two-pointer merge idea still applies, but since linked lists do not need pre-reserved space, a simple forward merge works directly, splicing nodes together without any overwrite risk at all.

How would you merge k sorted arrays instead of just 2? A pairwise merge repeated k minus 1 times works but is not optimal; a min-heap holding the current front of each array, always extracting the smallest, generalizes this two-pointer idea efficiently to many arrays at once.
Same two-pointer merge step as the merge phase of merge sort, just adapted to write in place instead of into a fresh auxiliary array.
Same "process from the safe end to avoid overwriting unread data" insight as in-place array compaction problems, such as removing duplicates or shifting elements without a second array.

Same "both sides already sorted, so avoid redoing that work" recognition that also applies to Squares of a Sorted Array and other two-pointer problems that exploit existing order instead of re-sorting.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O((m plus n) log(m plus n)) time, O(log(m plus n)) to O(m plus n) space.
Optimized (merge from the back): O(m plus n) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: Backward three-pointer merge of two sorted sequences sharing one in-place destination array
Core Idea: Since the unused space sits at the end of nums1, merge from the back, always placing the larger of the two current candidates, so nothing unread is ever overwritten
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: An in-place merge must proceed from whichever end holds the unused destination space, to guarantee no not-yet-read value is ever overwritten
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Fill from the back, largest first, since the back is where the empty room actually is
